Abstract 49 50 Background 51 The determinants of COVID-19 disease severity and extrapulmonary complications (EPCs) are 52 poorly understood. We characterise the relationships between SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia and 53 disease severity, clinical deterioration, and specific EPCs. 54 55 Methods 56 We used quantitative (qPCR) and digital (dPCR) PCR to quantify SARS-CoV-2 RNA from 57 nasopharyngeal swabs and plasma in 191 patients presenting to the Emergency Department (ED) 58 with COVID-19. We recorded patient symptoms, laboratory markers, and clinical outcomes, 59 with a focus on oxygen requirements over time. We collected longitudinal plasma samples from 60 a subset of patients. We characterised the role of RNAaemia in predicting clinical severity and 61 EPCs using elastic net regression. 62 63 Findings 64 23·0% (44/191) of SARS-CoV-2 positive patients had viral RNA detected in plasma by dPCR, 65 compared to 1·4% (2/147) by qPCR. Most patients with serial measurements had undetectable 66 RNAaemia 10 days after onset of symptoms, but took 16 days to reach maximum severity, and 67 33 days for symptoms to resolve. Initially RNAaemic patients were more likely to manifest 68 severe disease (OR 6·72 [95% CI, 2·45 – 19·79]), worsening of disease severity (OR 2·43 [95% 69 CI, 1·07 - 5·38]), and EPCs (OR 2·81 [95% CI, 1·26 – 6·36]). RNA load correlated with 70 maximum severity (r = 0·47 [95% CI, 0·20 - 0·67]). 71 72 Interpretation 73 dPCR is more sensitive than qPCR for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia, which is a 74 robust predictor of eventual COVID-19 severity and oxygen requirements, as well as EPCs. 75 Since many COVID-19 therapies are initiated on the basis of oxygen requirements, RNAaemia 76 on presentation might serve to direct early initiation of appropriate therapies for the patients most 77 likely to deteriorate. 78 79 Funding 80 NIH/NIAID (Grants R01A153133, R01AI137272, and 3U19AI057229 – 17W1 COVID SUPP 81 #2) and a donation from Eva Grove. 82 83 Acknowledgements 84 Additional author members of the Stanford COVID-19 Biobank Study Group include: Rosen 85 Mann, Anita Visweswaran, Thanmayi Ranganath, Jonasel Roque, Monali Manohar, Hena Naz 86 Din, Komal Kumar, Kathryn Jee, Brigit Noon, Jill Anderson, Bethany Fay, Donald Schreiber, 87 Nancy Zhao, Rosemary Vergara, Julia McKechnie, Aaron Wilk, Lauren de la Parte, Kathleen 88 Whittle Dantzler, Maureen Ty, Nimish Kathale, Arjun Rustagi, Giovanny Martinez-Colon, Geoff 89 Ivison, Ruoxi Pi, Maddie Lee, Rachel Brewer, Taylor Hollis, Andrea Baird, Michele Ugur, Drina 90 Bogusch, Georgie Nahass, Kazim Haider, Kim Quyen Thi Tran, Laura Simpson, Michal Tal, Iris 91 Chang, Evan Do, Andrea Fernandes, Allie Lee, Neera Ahuja, Theo Snow, James Krempski. 92 93 94

Research in context 95 96 Evidence before this study – 97 98 The varied clinical manifestations of COVID-19 have directed attention to the distribution of 99 SARS-CoV-2 in the body. Although most concentrated and tested for in the nasopharynx, 100 SARS-CoV-2 RNA has been found in blood, stool, and numerous tissues, raising questions about 101 dissemination of viral RNA throughout the body, and the role of this process in disease severity 102 and extrapulmonary complications. Recent studies have detected low levels of SARS-CoV-2 103 RNA in blood using either quantitative reverse transcriptase real-time PCR (qPCR) or droplet 104 digital PCR (dPCR), and have associated RNAaemia with disease severity and biomarkers of 105 dysregulated immune response. 106 107 Added value of this study – 108 109 We quantified SARS-CoV-2 RNA in the nasopharynx and plasma of patients presenting to the 110 Emergency Department with COVID-19, and found an array-based dPCR platform to be 111 markedly more sensitive than qPCR for detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA, with a simplified 112 workflow well-suited to clinical adoption. We collected serial plasma samples during patients’ 113 course of illness, and showed that SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia peaks early, while clinical condition 114 often continues to worsen. Our findings confirm the association between RNAaemia and disease 115 severity, and additionally demonstrate a role for RNAaemia in predicting future deterioration and 116 specific extrapulmonary complications. 117 118 Implications of all the available evidence – 119 120 Variation in SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia may help explain disparities in disease severity and 121 extrapulmonary complications from COVID-19. Testing for RNAaemia with dPCR early in the 122 course of illness may help guide patient triage and management. 123 124 Introduction 125 126 As of December 2020,  SARS-CoV-2 has caused over 70 million infections and 1·6 million 127 deaths.1 The variability of patient responses to COVID-19 makes it difficult for frontline 128 clinicians to identify and appropriately triage patients most at risk for clinical deterioration. 129 While COVID-19 is often manifest as a viral pneumonia, multi-organ involvement can produce 130 more severe and recalcitrant disease.2,3 SARS-CoV-2, typically isolated from nasopharyngeal 131 (NP) samples, has been detected in lower titers in whole blood, serum, plasma, and stool.4–10 132 Histopathological surveys have identified the virus in myocardial, renal, gastrointestinal, and 133 neurological tissues.11–14 Is haematogenous spread of the virus or viral components associated 134 with extrapulmonary complications (EPCs)? The clinical and pathophysiological significance of 135 SARS-CoV-2 RNA in blood remains poorly understood. 136 137 SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia, detected with quantitative reverse transcriptase real-time PCR 138 (qPCR), has been correlated with severity of COVID-19. However, reported rates of RNA 139 detection range from 0% – 41% in serum and 13% – 33% in plasma.4,6,7,10,15–17 Comparing across 140

Conventional qPCR also lacks the sensitivity and precision to 142 reliably detect and measure low viral loads.18 Digital PCR (dPCR) offers improved sensitivity, 143 precision, and reproducibility over qPCR, with absolute quantification of viral RNA without 144 standard curves. Given its tolerance to inhibitors, dPCR is particularly suited to detecting dilute 145 targets in blood.19 Two cross-sectional studies using droplet-based dPCR reported higher rates of 146 RNAaemia (42·4% and 74·1%) than did the qPCR studies above, and associated the presence 147 and the level of RNAaemia with clinical severity.8,9 Bermejo-Martin et al also observed 148 correlation between RNAaemia and biomarkers of dysregulated host responses.8 149 150 In this prospective, longitudinal, observational study of COVID-19 patients presenting to the 151 Emergency Department (ED), we characterised relationships between SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia 152 and overall severity, clinical deterioration, and specific EPCs. We used an array-based dPCR 153 platform to maximise reliability and replicability, and to simplify potential clinical adoption of 154 RNAaemia testing. 155 156 Materials and Methods 157 158 COVID-19 patients and specimen collection - 159 160 We collected peripheral blood +/- NP swabs from patients prospectively enrolled in the IRB- 161 approved (eP-55650) Stanford University ED COVID-19 Biobank beginning in April 2020, after 162 written informed consent from patients or their surrogates. Eligibility criteria were age ≥18 years 163 and presentation to the Stanford Hospital ED with a positive screening SARS-CoV-2 NP swab, 164 analysed by RT-PCR as part of routine ED care. We repeated blood draws on one or more of 165 days three, seven and 30 if the patient remained hospitalised. We asked discharged participants 166 to return for repeat blood draws on days seven and 30 from enrollment. We collected blood in 167 ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid-chelated vacutainers (Becton, Dickinson, and Co.). We isolated, 168 aliquoted, and stored plasma at -80°C after centrifugation at 1200g for ten minutes at 25°C. We 169 collected NP swabs in 1·5mL of RNA Shield Stabilizing Solution (Zymo Research) and stored 170 solution at -80°C. We performed all sample processing under biosafety level 2+ precautions as 171 approved by Stanford University APB-2551. 172 173 SARS-CoV-2 RNA extraction - 174 175 We extracted RNA from research NP swab and plasma using the QIAamp Viral RNA Mini Kit 176 and QIACube Connect (QIAGEN). We used 140µL of NP swab suspension or plasma as input 177 and eluted RNA in 50µL of elution buffer after lysing for 10 minutes before transferring to 178 QIACube connect. 179 180 SARS-CoV-2 RNA detection and quantification - 181 182 Multiplexed qPCR and dPCR reactions included the extracted RNA, |Q| Triplex Assay 183 (Combinati), and 4x RT-dPCR MM (Combinati). The |Q| Triplex Assay (Combinati) included 184 primers and probes targeting the N1 and N2 regions of the nucleoprotein gene and the human 185 ribonuclease P gene (RP). We divided the reaction mixture as follows: 10µL for qPCR using the 186

Every qPCR and dPCR run included a non- 188 template control (NTC) extracted using the QIACube (NTC-QIA), NTC for PCR, positive 189 extraction control using a combination of the SARS-CoV-2 Specimen positive and negative 190 recombinants (Zeptometrix Corporation), and a positive PCR control with the SARS-CoV-2 191 Standard from Exact Diagnostics. 192 193 We considered a qPCR specimen to be positive if cycle threshold (Ct) for RP, N1, and N2 were 194 all less than 40. For positive samples, we used the lesser (i.e., more readily detected) of N1/N2 195 Ct for quantitative analysis. We repeated qPCR if the Ct value for RP was greater than 40. We 196 defined a dPCR sample as positive if both N1 and N2 were detected at concentrations of at least 197 0·23 copies/µL, and used the larger of the two concentrations for quantitative analysis. We set 198 negative qPCR results to 40 (our Ct threshold), and negative dPCR results to zero. We calculated 199 pairwise Pearson’s correlations between measures of qPCR Ct and log-transformed RNA 200 concentrations from dPCR. 201 202 Patients with specimens collected on days after enrollment (day zero) typically had specimens 203 collected on day three or seven, not both. Thus, we combined days three and seven (hereafter day 204 3/7) for purposes of sequential analyses. For patients who had the same test performed on both 205 days, we used the greater of the two values. 206 207 Clinical and laboratory measures - 208 209 For all participants, we recorded clinical severity of COVID-19 on enrollment and at the time of 210 every additional blood draw, and noted the maximum severity attributable to COVID-19 for 30 211 days after each patient’s enrollment, using a World Health Organization (WHO) COVID-19 212 severity scale modified for our institution’s COVID-19 oxygenation protocols: 1 = asymptomatic 213 infection not requiring admission, 2 = symptomatic infection not requiring admission, 3 = 214 admitted without supplemental oxygen, 4 = admitted, requiring oxygen by nasal cannula, 5 = 215 admitted, requiring oxygen by high-flow nasal cannula, 6 = admitted, requiring mechanical 216 ventilation, 7 = admitted, requiring mechanical ventilation and vasopressors or renal replacement 217 therapy, 8 = death from COVID-related cause.20 We also clustered scores as mild (1-2), 218 moderate (3-4), and severe (5-8). Patients were considered to have neurologic involvement if they were diagnosed with 251 one or more of: acute stroke, encephalitis, meningitis, neuroinflammatory disease, delirium. 252 Cardiovascular involvement included myocardial injury, acute coronary syndrome, 253 cardiomyopathy, acute cor pulmonale, arrhythmia, or cardiogenic shock. Patients were considered to have immunologic involvement if they received a 258 diagnosis of sepsis, septic shock, multi-organ failure, or secondary bacterial infection. 259 260 Characterising associations between RNAaemia and clinical severity - 261 262 We calculated mean maximum WHO severity scores for patients who were initially RNAaemic 263 and non-RNAaemic, and compared mean scores with a two-sample t-test. Among RNAaemic 264 patients, we calculated Pearson’s correlation between log-transformed concentration of RNA in 265 plasma, and maximal clinical severity (WHO 1-8). We calculated proportions of RNAaemic and 266 non-RNAaemic patients who manifested mild (WHO 1-2), moderate (WHO 3-4), and severe 267 (WHO 5-8) disease, who were admitted to the hospital, who manifested EPCs, and who 268 worsened after presentation (i.e., had a maximum WHO score exceeding WHO score at 269 enrollment). We compared the proportions of RNAaemic and non-RNAaemic patients in each of 270 those categories using chi-squared tests with continuity corrections. We calculated the odds ratio 271 for clinical deterioration, by RNAaemia on enrollment (using the odds ratio for consistency with 272 logistic regression results), and calculated exact 95% confidence intervals.21 We compared 273 median length-of-hospitalisation in days, and median degree of clinical worsening (difference 274 between initial and maximum WHO score), for RNAaemic and non-RNAaemic patients, using 275 the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with continuity correction to compare these distributions. 276 277 Predictive models for severe disease, extrapulmonary complications, and RNAaemia - 278

279 We developed a predictive model for severe (WHO 5-8) disease, based on data available upon 280 patient presentation. We included the following variables as potential predictors of severe 281 disease: demographic features, comorbidities, binary indicators of abnormal ED vital signs, 282 pneumonia on chest X-ray or CT, patient-reported symptoms, and binary indicators of abnormal 283 lab values (described above). Because therapies such as Remdesivir and dexamethasone were 284 generally initiated after ED presentation, and on the basis of oxygen requirements (the main 285 constituent of the WHO severity score), we did not include specific treatments in our predictive 286 models. 287 288 To prevent overfitting, given a large number of potential predictors compared to the number of 289 patients, we selected variables via elastic net regularisation (glmnet 4·0 in R), using logistic 290 models and 10-fold cross-validation, selecting the regularisation parameter λ minimising mean 291 cross-validated error. We then used the selected variables in a logistic model, and estimated odds 292 ratios and 95% confidence intervals for prediction of severe disease, for each of the selected 293 features. We calculated mean cross-validated area under the receiver-operating characteristic 294 curve (AUROC) of the resulting model. 295 296 We predicted the presence of EPCs in analogous fashion, excluding the patient-reported 297 symptoms potentially constitutive of EPCs as defined above, and excluding laboratory markers, 298 many of which were used in definition of EPCs. We again selected variables via cross-validated 299 elastic-net regularisation, estimated odds ratios for the most robust predictors of EPCs, and 300 characterised overall predictive accuracy by AUROC. 301 302 Finally, we predicted the presence of RNAaemia in analogous fashion, using as potential 303 predictors demographic features, comorbidities, and symptoms, but excluding radiographic and 304 laboratory findings. 305 306 Results 307 308 Patient characteristics on enrollment - 309 310 We enrolled 191 COVID-19 positive ED patients, all of whom had plasma sampled on day of 311 enrollment (day zero). In an 404 analogous regularised, cross-validated logistic model (Table S1), significant predictors of 405 RNAaemia on presentation were limited to cough and hypoxia, though the overall predictive 406 performance of the model was poor (mean cross-validated AUROC 0·66). 407 408 Discussion 409 410 The pathogenesis of COVID-19, its temporal dynamics, and the determinants of disease severity 411 and extrapulmonary complications are incompletely understood. We explored the performance 412 and clinical utility of dPCR in quantifying SARS-CoV-2 RNA in the nasopharynx and plasma, 413 and characterised the relationships between RNAaemia and disease severity, clinical 414 deterioration, and extrapulmonary complications. Array-based dPCR was much more sensitive 415 than qPCR for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 in plasma, where mean concentration of viral RNA 416

was three orders of magnitude less than in the nasopharynx. RNAaemia manifests early in the 417 course of illness, while clinical manifestations peak later and are more prolonged. RNAaemia at 418 presentation predicts severe disease, ongoing clinical deterioration, and specific extrapulmonary 419 complications. 420 421 We found dPCR to be markedly more sensitive than qPCR even while using more stringent 422 detection criteria (both N1 and N2 >=0·23 copies/µL) than other studies (e.g., either N1 or N2 423 >=0·1 copies/µL).8 dPCR was also more consistent in multiplex detection of both regions (N1 424 and N2) of the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid gene, likely related to the partition format in dPCR 425 reducing preferential amplifications often observed in bulk PCR.22 Moreover, a dPCR platform 426 based on microwell array enhances partition consistency, minimises dead volume for improved 427 sensitivity, and has a workflow identical to qPCR, making it suitable for incorporation into 428 existing clinical workflows. Early in the course of an outbreak, before viral RNA standard curves 429 are widely available, dPCR is a natural choice for detecting a novel pathogen. 430 431 RNAaemia on presentation was a major predictor of both severe disease and extrapulmonary 432 complications, after accounting for demographics, comorbidities, symptoms, vital signs, and a 433 host of laboratory markers. Moreover, RNAaemic patients were more likely than non-RNAaemic 434 patients to worsen after presentation, and RNAaemic patients who worsened did so by a greater 435 degree. Previous studies have associated RNAaemia with disease severity and mortality.8,10,23 436 Reported associations between RNAaemia and extrapulmonary involvement are more 437 varied.2,24,25 In addition to characterising the temporal dynamics of clinical deterioration, we 438 included a more comprehensive scope of potential confounders than previous studies.8 We also 439 use cross-validation not only for model selection, but to assess the relative predictability of 440 clinical severity (good, AUROC 0·82), extrapulmonary complications (fair, AUROC 0·73), and 441 RNAaemia itself (poor, AUROC 0·66). The poor predictability of RNAaemia from patient 442 features observable on initial presentation, and the weak correlations between NP and plasma 443 measurements of SARS-CoV-2 RNA, suggest that RNAaemia is not simply a consequence of 444 sufficient viral load at the typical site of inoculation, but may instead signal unique 445 pathophysiologic and prognostic features.6,26,27 446 447 SARS-CoV-2 RNAaemia might arise from spillage from the respiratory tract, or from active 448 viral replication in vascular endothelial or perivascular cells.28,29 Whether RNAaemia represents 449 intact, replicating virus cannot be directly determined from our data, and an attempt to culture 450 SARS-CoV-2 from serum with low RNA levels was not successful.30 SARS-CoV-1, however, 451 has been found to replicate in circulating lymphocytes, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic 452 cells.31–33 The RNAaemia kinetics we observed follow a typical viral kinetic pattern, with high 453 peak viral load early in the infection, followed by rapid decay (likely reflecting the innate 454 immune response), before a slower clearance (from acquired immunity).34 RNAaemia prior to 455 symptom onset has been anecdotally reported; more data is needed to better assess potential pre- 456 symptomatic dynamics.30 Since our findings suggest that RNAaemia on presentation reflects the 457 likelihood of subsequent disease progression, early testing for RNAaemia could prove useful for 458 the targeted initiation and monitoring of antiviral therapies.34 459 460 The association we observed between RNAaemia and EPCs (which we defined conservatively 461 based on diagnoses at discharge, rather than surrogate biomarkers alone), is stronger than in 462
